newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK unemployment tumbles to seven-year low.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK unemployment tumbles to seven-year low.

text.p: British unemployment tumbled to a seven-year low in June, official figures on Wednesday showed, but the financial markets were more impressed by a drop in wage growth.
The Office for National Statistics said the number of unemployed dropped 36,500 to 1.6 million last month, the lowest since April 1990. The 5.7-percent jobless rate was the lowest since August 1990.
Unemployment has been falling consistently in recent years and spectacularly in recent months so, few analysts were surprised by another cut in the dole queues.
But a drop in annual average earnings growth to 4.25 percent in May, from 4.5 the month before, was a shock.
The FTSE-100 index of leading shares leapt more than 50 points to a new record of 4,950 after the figures, and government bonds rallied.

Employment minister Andrew Smith said Labour's welfare-to-work scheme, aimed at finding skilled jobs for 250,000 young out-of-work people, would help keep wages down and further cut the jobless total.
"By adding to the supply of skilled labour, we can avoid the inflationary bottlenecks of the past," he said.
Traditionally in Britain, low unemployment fuels wage inflation as companies looking to hire, face a skills shortage and have to pay more for the workers they want.

"The labour market continues to get tighter and yet, there is no sign that average earnings is picking up," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International. "Although the economy continues to push ahead, and there is a case for suggesting that inflationary pressures are building at the moment, there is no sign that those pressures are actually occurring."
The Trades Union Congress, while welcoming the drop in unemployment, said a sky-high pound and rapidly rising interest rates would cost jobs in the future.
"The high value of the pound and interest rates puts a question mark over hundreds of thousands of manufacturing jobs in the future," Bill Callaghan, the TUC's chief economist, said.
The pound has surged by almost 25 percent since last August against other major currencies and has sprinted further in recent weeks, helped by three interest rate rises in as many months.
Minutes from the first meeting of the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee, released at the same time as the jobs figures, showed all members present agreed to raise base rates in June.
Another rise was agreed last week, taking rates to 6.75 percent. Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown gave the central bank freedom to set interest rates shortly after Labour took power on May 1.
The minutes showed the panel saw a rise in wage growth since late 1995, when earnings were only rising by 3.25 percent, as evidence of a tightening labour market.

But City economists thought Wednesday's earnings data may persuade the central bank to hold rates steady for at least the next month. "The average earnings numbers have increased the chances that the next rise in interest rates will be in September rather than August," said Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers.
June public sector debt figures were also released on Wednesday. They showed a public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) of 4.75 billion stg, well above forecasts for 4.0 billion.
But that does not mean public finances are suddenly deteriorating. The ONS said interest payments on British government bonds have been reorganised so they now fall due mainly in June and December.

As a result, 2.7 billion stg in coupon payments were paid last month, compared with 1.5 billion in June 1996. Also, alteration of VAT (value-addded tax) payment times meant government coffers were deprived of 400 million pounds last month.
"I'd expect to see the PSBR bounce back in the months to come," said David Philpotts, economist at Schroders.
